title: UN climate fund promises $20 million for Nepal flood recovery, far short of billions needed - Bozeman Daily Chronicle
description: UN climate fund promises $20 million for Nepal flood recovery, far short of billions needed  Bozeman Daily Chronicle
publisher.title: Bozeman Daily Chronicle
full_article:
BENGALURU, India (AP) — A United Nations climate fund has provisionally set aside $20 million to help Nepal recover from catastrophic flooding that killed more than 1,400 people, left thousands missing and caused billions of dollars in damage to homes, schools and hydropower dams in the Himalayan country and in China.

Nepalese government officials and climate policy experts welcomed the move, but said the $20 million represents only a fraction of the $4.7 billion the government estimates is needed for recovery and reconstruction.

“It’s a very small amount compared to what we lost,” said Maheshwar Dhakal, a senior official in Nepal’s climate and environment ministry. But Dhakal said that releasing the money sends a significant message: “This shows that the global community can take the right decision at the right time to help those who are most vulnerable to climate change.”





The government said it had received around $102 million from domestic and international donors as of the end of September. Dhakal said the government is working with neighboring countries like India and China, as well as multilateral development banks, to raise more of the money it needs for recovery.

It's the first payout from a UN fund to respond to climate disasters

The U.N. Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage approved the payout — the fund's first — at an emergency board meeting Thursday.

The fund is aimed at providing assistance to countries hit by climate change. It was created at the 2022 U.N. climate talks following years of demands from vulnerable developing nations, which contribute relatively little to emissions of planet-warming gases but often bear some of the worst consequences.

Countries have pledged more than $820 million to the fund, while it faces 176 requests for support from developing nations totaling about $2.8 billion. The fund’s board members will meet in December to consider more support requests.

The next round of U.N. climate negotiations is scheduled to begin in Turkey next month, and financing for countries impacted by climate-related disasters is expected to be a key issue.

Climate change helped fuel Nepal floods

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah, speaking at the United Nations in September, said Nepal was paying a devastating price for a crisis it had barely contributed to causing.

“We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying a colossal price for it,” he said.

Human-caused climate change was a key factor in destabilizing the mountainside whose collapse triggered the devastating flood.

An analysis by the World Weather Attribution research group released in September found that warming temperatures had thinned glaciers and thawed permafrost, weakening the ice and frozen ground that helped hold mountain rock in place.

Climate scientists said that rising temperatures are causing glaciers to retreat across the Himalayas and thawing permanently frozen ground that helps bind fractured mountain rock together.

The Himalayan region contains the largest volume of snow and ice outside the polar regions. More than 63,000 glaciers in the area feed at least 10 major Asian river systems and support the food, water, energy and livelihood security of billions of people. However, studies have found that around 78% of the glacier area, which is located between 4,500 and 6,000 meters (14,763 to 19,685 feet) above sea level, is highly exposed to warming. United Nations reports have found that between 2000 and 2019, glaciers lost 267 billion tons of ice per year.

International aid cuts deepen crisis for climate-vulnerable countries

Massive cuts to international aid budgets, including that of the United States Agency for International Development, have made it harder for countries like Nepal to prepare and respond to climate-driven disasters, said climate experts.

“The (U.N.) loss and damage fund’s response to the floods is now demonstrating, in equally devastating fashion, the utter inadequacy of support from rich countries for countries like Nepal,” said Brandon Wu, policy and campaigns director at ActionAid USA.

Official development assistance from major donor countries fell 23% in 2025 according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. The United States led the reductions, while Germany, the United Kingdom, France and Japan also cut aid spending.

“The reality is that we need trillions of dollars every year, but developed countries have not met their obligation,” said Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign, a global group that pressures governments to contribute to the U.N. fund.

Singh called for a permanent mechanism capable of delivering emergency climate assistance quickly, rather than forcing disaster-hit countries through lengthy approval processes.

“Nepal needs billions to rebuild, and this Fund is responding only in millions,” he said.

The funding shortfall is expected to intensify demands at the upcoming U.N. climate talks for richer countries to increase their financial commitments.

full_article:
KATHMANDU: Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle held direct talks with Indian External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar on Nepal-India relations and regional issues during the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi, India.

Speaking at a session titled “A World Between Orders,” Wagle praised India’s assistance to Nepal during recent disasters.

According to the Ministry of Finance, Wagle referred to the recent disasters in Rasuwa and Bhotekoshi linked to climate change, as well as India’s support following Nepal’s devastating 2015 earthquake.

“As a Nepali minister, I can say that India was present within the first few hours during both the recent disasters and the earthquake, providing us with extraordinary support,” Wagle said. “Nepal is deeply grateful for this assistance.”

Wagle also highlighted the potential for institutionalizing cooperation at bilateral, trilateral, and sub-regional levels in areas including disaster response, nutrition, and clean energy.

Responding to the proposal, Indian External Affairs Minister Jaishankar emphasized the importance of formal institutional frameworks wherever feasible, citing the International Solar Alliance as an example.

However, he noted that like-minded countries have increasingly been adopting flexible approaches to cooperation, pursuing initiatives as needed and placing greater emphasis on achieving tangible results.

title: What is the importance of the UN Loss and Damage Fund’s payout to Nepal? | Explained - The Hindu
description: What is the importance of the UN Loss and Damage Fund’s payout to Nepal? | Explained  The Hindu
publisher.title: The Hindu
full_article:
Story so far: The United Nations’ climate convention’s Loss and Damage Fund has approved a $21.6 million pay out (approx. ₹205 crore) to the Nepal government to help with rebuilding, following the devastating floods in August.

What is the UN Loss and Damage Fund?

Formally, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), was set up to help developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to climate change respond to economic and non-economic losses, including from extreme weather and slow-onset events. It operates under the financial mechanism of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Governments agreed to create it at COP27 in 2022, and its Governing Instrument was adopted at COP28 in 2023.

Nepal’s flash floods: How can communities rebuild after a disaster?

As of March 15, 2026, 27 countries had pledged $822.06 million (approx. ₹7,809.6 crore), with $629.70 million (₹5,982 crore) in grant contributions. Its start-up allocation is $342 million with at least half of it reserved for small island developing States and least developed countries. Its first call for funding requests drew 176 requests from 119 countries worth about $2.8 billion (₹26,600 crore). In July the Board deferred decisions on those requests to December.

What is the significance of this decision?

It is the first time the Fund has earmarked money for a specific country. The Board took the decision at its first “extraordinary meeting,” held virtually on October 22, 2026. It also agreed to pilot, during the start-up phase, an approach allowing Nepal to submit a request outside the closed submission window. Any further such submissions will need separate Board decisions, and the Secretariat will assess lessons for the Fund’s long-term model.

Villages evacuated as flash flood from Budhi Gandaki River hits northern Nepal

On August 26, 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche, that experts say is linked to climate changed from human-accelerated global warming, set off flooding along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. Nepal estimates economic losses of at least $2.69 billion and recovery needs of at least $4.71 billion. The decision comes weeks before COP31 opens in Turkiye.

How does the money pay out?

The $21.6 million approved by the Board includes $1.6 million in oversight fees, which are paid to the organisations that implement projects to cover the cost of supervising how money is used. Nepal has been invited to submit a funding request, which the Board will consider at its tenth meeting in Manila in December. Money would be released only after that approval.

The Fund has not publicly said how much cash it holds beyond signed contributions, and disbursement depends on donors honouring pledges.

Why has the Fund faced questions about its credibility?

Since its creation at COP27, the Fund has had to show that pledges translate into money for affected countries. The United States, the largest historical emitter, had pledged $17.5 million under President Joe Biden. In January 2025, the Trump administration withdrew the US representatives from the Fund’s board which was part of the US’ larger exit out of the Paris Agreement. At the time, pledges stood at about $741 million.

Nepal flash floods wash away illusions of clean, easy hydropower

Jawad Khalid, a climate finance specialist writing for the Lowy Institute, an independent Australian think tank, argued that the Fund “still operates like a conventional development fund” rather than an emergency mechanism. “Its single funding cycle runs eleven steps, from origination through technical review to board approval. The Fund is hosted by the World Bank, which serves as its interim trustee,” he wrote in a piece.

What concerns have experts raised following the approval?

Ajay Mathur, a former Director General of the International Solar Alliance, called the step “landmark” in a media statement. He cautioned that the sum is less than 0.5 per cent of Nepal’s estimated $5 billion reconstruction cost. He noted that cash would flow only after further project proposals are cleared, risking delays to relief.

Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, said in a media statement that while the Fund “took a historic first step” it it “cannot be a one-off.” He said no country should have to wait seven weeks, through “historic letters and relentless pressure,” to unlock an emergency meeting, and called for a permanent rapid-response system that moves support “in days, not months.” He said developed countries insisted the decision must not set a precedent or prejudge the long-term model, adding: “Nepal needs billions to rebuild, and this Fund is responding only in millions.”

Others read the decision more positively. Raju Pandit Chhetri, the Least Developed Countries’ lead climate finance negotiator, said it showed countries could reach “swift, effective consensus” and set “a strong precedent.”

title: Bodies of Missing Japanese Climbers Found on Gangapurna West - Explorersweb »
description: Bodies of Missing Japanese Climbers Found on Gangapurna West  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
This morning, rescuers found the bodies of Japanese climbers Hidesuke Taneishi, 40, and Tetsu Hashimoto, 25, on Gangapurna West (7,140m).

“Both bodies were found at around 6,300m on the south side of Gangapurna West,” the rescue team told The Tourism Times .

Hidesuke Taneishi (left) and Tetsu Hashimoto (right) with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure

The climbers were attempting the first ascent of the mountain and lost contact on October 15 at approximately 7,050m on their summit push.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Heli/drone search

A search and rescue team has been looking for the pair since October 19. Unfortunately, no one knew where they were on the mountain, or even if they were on the mountain at all. Therefore, the search started at Manang village, with no success.

The team included helicopter pilot Sobit Gauchan, high-altitude photographer and climber Manish Maharjan, and IFMGA mountain guide Pasang Rinzi Sherpa. The helicopter dropped Maharjan and Rinzi at 5,750m, and from there they used a drone to search the upper slopes. They scouted the northeast and southwest sides of the mountain, and finally found the remains of the Japanese climbers’ higher camp. Today, they found the bodies on the south side.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Background

Several teams have attempted Gangapurna West, located next to the Annapurna massif in Manang district, since it opened to foreign teams in 2014. However, none have summited. The mountain is also known as Asapurna or Lachenal Peak.

Team leader Hidesuke Taneishi was nominated for a Piolet d’Or last year after his first ascent of 6,652m Pholesobi Peak, also in Nepal, via a direct route up its vertiginous north face with Hiroki Yamamoto.

Twenty years after a helicopter crash killed some of Nepal’s most prominent environmental figures, the nation is celebrating ecological gains while grappling with a void in visionary leadership, reports Mongabay’s Abhaya Raj Joshi.

On Sept. 23, 2006, a Russian-built Mi-8 helicopter crashed near the high-altitude mountain village of Ghunsa, killing all 20 passengers and four crew members . The victims included Gopal Rai , the minister of forests and soil conservation; other senior government officials; a Finnish diplomat; a USAID official; and key WWF staff. They had traveled to Ghunsa to hand over management of the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area, in the northeastern corner of Nepal, to local communities. The crash occurred the next day as the group was taking off from Ghunsa.

“For the community, this was the beginning,” said Ghana Shyam Gurung, now country representative for WWF Nepal. Seven WWF staff died in the crash, the single greatest loss of life in the history of the organization.

Among them were Harka Gurung, Chandra Gurung, and Mingma Norbu Sherpa, and their loss left an institutional vacuum.

“We didn’t just lose people that day. We lost the pace we were moving at,”

said Sarita Jnawali, a former conservationist with the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC).

Shiv Raj Bhatta, an ecologist at the Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation, who lost key supervisors in the crash, recalled the immediate aftershock. “I wondered how we would ever produce people of that height again,” Bhatta said.

The community-based conservation framework championed by that generation laid the groundwork for major ecological gains over the next two decades.

Nepal’s forest cover expanded from roughly 40% in the 1990s to more than 46% today , driven by more than 23,000 community forest groups managing 2.5 million hectares (6.2 million acres) of land. And the country’s tiger population more than tripled from 121 in 2010 to 429 this year . The rhino population grew from 645 in 2015 to 752 in 2021 .

But these population recoveries also brought challenges.

A 2026 study of Nepal’s Terai Arc Landscape documented 245 tiger attacks on humans between 2010 and 2024, with 141 fatalities. In Taplejung district, site of the 2006 helicopter crash, data from Phungling municipality point to up to 330 families abandoning their hill settlements amid crop losses by monkeys.

Former forest ministry secretary Krishna Chandra Paudel described the loss as “a wound that left a deep scar,” adding that official government commemorations have largely lapsed over the past decade.

WWF’s Gurung said conservation in Nepal needs a breakthrough on the scale of the 1990s shift to community-based management, one built around climate and water. “The world ahead is about water,” he said.

• The Board of the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) has provisionally set aside $21.6 million from its available commitment authority for Nepal.

• The decision was made during the Board’s first-ever extraordinary meeting on October 22.

• The Board has 26 members from Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and the 2015 Paris Agreement.

• Triggered by a climate-induced ice-and-rock avalanche on August 26, a massive debris flow and severe downstream flooding devastated Nepal’s Bhote Koshi-Trishuli-Narayani river system, claiming many lives and leaving others still missing.

What is FRLD?

• Climate change disproportionately affects developing nations, leading to excessive losses and damage, undermining development progress, exacerbating poverty, displacing populations, and destabilising livelihoods.

• The Conference of the Parties (COP) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement (CMA) established the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) with a mandate to assist developing nations that are particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change in responding to economic and non-economic loss and damage associated with the adverse effects of climate change, including extreme weather events and slow onset events.

• A landmark agreement reached at COP27 in 2022 in Sharm El-Sheikh, Egypt, led to the decision to establish a fund to consolidate global efforts to address climate-induced loss and damage.

• Subsequently, a transitional committee was formed to help design the Fund’s framework.

• During COP28 in 2023 in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates, the COP and CMA decided to operationalise the Fund as an entity entrusted with the operation of the financial mechanism.

• It addresses the growing needs of vulnerable communities in developing countries facing the irreversible impacts of climate change.

• By financing recovery initiatives from climate-related losses and damage, the Fund empowers communities to rebuild and adapt.

• It strives for country-led locally driven solutions, ensuring interventions are aligned to country needs, priorities and contexts.

• A Board of 26 members was constituted in 2023, and subsequently, the Philippines was selected as the host of the Board in 2024, while the World Bank was selected to host the Secretariat, and as the Fund Trustee.

full_article:
Last Updated on October 23, 2026 4:24 pm by INDIAN AWAAZ

By Manan Kumar

The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal and Uttarkashi in the Himalayan region which claimed more than thounsand lives and left thousands missing, serve as a grim warning of what lies ahead. Geologists and climate scientists have warned that a strengthening El Niño cycle, superimposed on decades of accelerated global warming, could trigger an early and exceptionally intense summer across India, Nepal, and China in the summer of 2027.

Many experts like Professor Anil Kulkarni, leading glaciologist at the Divecha Centre for Climate Change Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and Saswat Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) have warned that rapid temperature increases and human-driven warming in the Himalayas will significantly raise the frequency of such catastrophic disasters.

This extreme thermal stress is expected to destabilize the high-altitude cryosphere (part of the Earth’s surface where water is in solid form, including ice, snow, glaciers, ice caps, ice sheets, and frozen ground) accelerating permafrost degradation, rapid glacial melting, and unprecedented slope instability. Consequently, the whole Himalayan region faces a heightened risk of cascading mountain hazards, including massive rock-ice avalanches, landslides, and catastrophic Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) during the ensuing monsoon season.

The Geography of Vulnerability

According to the Centre of Science and Environment (CSE) the rapid warming of the Western Himalayas is outpacing global averages resulting in the thawing of the deep permafrost that holds steep mountain walls together. Without this frozen structural glue, the risk of massive rockfalls, landslides, and debris flows spikes dramatically during summer.

The threat in the Himalayan region is not uniform. Certain geographic zones are highly vulnerable to these compounding climate drivers. In India, the states of Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, and Sikkim are on high alert. The Teesta River basin in Sikkim remains fragile following the devastating South Lhonak lake burst, while Uttarakhand’s steep valleys—home to major pilgrimage routes and massive infrastructure projects—face persistent landslide risks.

In Nepal, the risk is concentrated in the steep, narrow valleys of the Koshi, Gandaki, and Karnali river systems. Densely populated settlements situated downstream from rapidly expanding moraine-dammed lakes are highly exposed. For China, the Tibetan Plateau acts as the primary ground zero. Rising temperatures are causing rapid thermal erosion of Tibet’s high-altitude permafrost, which directly threatens critical regional transport links like the Qinghai-Tibet railway, alongside local engineering infrastructure.

The danger is amplified by the fact that these hazards are intrinsically transboundary. A glacial lake outburst or mountain collapse originating in the high-altitude valleys of Tibet in China can transform into a destructive flood wave within minutes, roaring through the deep gorges of Nepal and India before downstream populations can receive adequate warning.

Early Warning Systems are not enough

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has expanded its network to include dozens of Doppler weather radars, which significantly improve the tracking of localized cloudburst events. The regional digital portals like the Sachet and Flood Watch applications push automated, geo-fenced alerts to mobile users in vulnerable zones.

However, these systems cannot provide alerts before or at the exact time of flash-floods and are inadequate for the scale of the impending crises. High-altitude structural collapses and flash floods hurtle down steep vertical drops at immense speeds. During recent monsoon disasters, official alerts were generated only after monitoring stations were physically disrupted, giving downstream communities very little time to evacuate.

Furthermore, the lack of continuous, automated ground instrumentation at high elevations creates significant data scarcity. The most critical gap is institutional: the absence of a real-time, automated, cross-border data pipeline between China, Nepal, and India prevents early warnings from crossing political borders at the speed required to save lives.

A Tri-National Strategy for Mitigation

To prevent future calamities from culminating in widespread tragedy, the governments of India, Nepal, and China must move past political friction and establish an integrated, proactive disaster mitigation framework. Disaster management organizations like the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) emphasise that cross-border cooperation is essential for managing systemic climate risks in mountain ecosystems.

The three nations must formalize a binding, real-time hydrological data-sharing treaty. The current practice of sharing seasonal or manually transmitted data during emergencies is insufficient. Automated weather and water-level stations positioned near dangerous glacial lakes in Tibet and northern Nepal must be digitally linked directly to downstream emergency operation centers in India and lower Nepal, ensuring that an upstream surge triggers an instantaneous, automated broadcast to downstream villages.

Second, the three governments must pool resources to deploy advanced cryosphere tracking technologies. Utilizing high-resolution satellite Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) interferometry and frequent drone surveys will allow geologists to map micro-cracks and structural displacement in high-risk slopes before they completely fail. Identifying these structural weaknesses early provides the weeks of lead time necessary to conduct planned evacuations.

Third, engineering interventions must be scaled up to stabilize high-risk glacial lakes. This requires constructing controlled structural drainage channels, siphoning systems, and spillways to safely lower water volumes in unstable moraine-dammed lakes. Such projects require shared technical expertise and joint funding across borders, as stabilizing a lake in Tibet directly secures infrastructure and lives downriver in India and Nepal.

Finally, geologists and structural engineers working in the Himalayas agree that all three nations must implement strict, risk-informed land-use zoning. Mountain development must change fundamentally. Governments need to enforce strict expert moratoria on the construction of heavy infrastructure, including dense chains of run-of-the-river hydropower projects and massive highway expansions, above highly vulnerable elevations. In steep valleys, residential and tourism infrastructure must be moved to higher ground, well above the natural choke points where flash floods concentrate vertically.

Only through coordinated, transparent, and immediate tri-national action can the nations of the Himalaya protect their shared environment, infrastructure, and people.
